title: Λύκος ⟨διὰ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ σκιὰν γαυρωθείς⟩ καὶ λέων
titleEn: The Wolf Made Proud by His Own Shadow, and the Lion
part: The Wolf Made Proud by His Own Shadow, and the Lion (Chambry 219)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 219. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t:
Λύκος πλανώμενος ⟨ποτ’⟩ ἐν ἐρήμοις τόποις,
κλίνοντος ἤδη πρὸς δύσιν Ὑπερίονος,
δολιχὴν ἑαυτοῦ τὴν σκιὰν ἰδὼν ἔφη·
« Λέοντ’ ἐγὼ δέδοικα, τηλικοῦτος ὤν ;
πλέθρου τ’ ἔχων τὸ μῆκος, οὐ θηρῶν ἁπλῶς
πάντων δυνάστης ἀθρόων γενήσομαι ; »
sentences.tr:
Lykos planōmenos ⟨pot’⟩ en erēmois topois,
klinontos ēdē pros dysin Hyperionos,
dolichēn heautou tēn skian idōn ephē·
« Leont’ egō dedoika, tēlikoutos ōn ;
plethrou t’ echōn to mēkos, ou thērōn haplōs
pantōn dynastēs athroōn genēsomai ; »
sentences.l: A wolf wandering ⟨once⟩ in desolate places, Hyperion already sinking toward his setting, having seen his own shadow long, said: « A lion — do I fear one, being of such a size? And having the length of a plethron, shall I not become lord of quite all the beasts together? »
sentences.i: A wolf was wandering once in desolate country, with the Sun already sinking toward his setting, and seeing how long his own shadow was he said: « Am I to fear a lion, big as I am? A hundred feet from end to end — shall I not become lord of every last beast at once? »
sentences.n: Chambry prints this fable as verse, not as prose like its neighbours, and the diction matches: Ὑπερίων is the Sun under his old poetic name, and the elisions Λέοντ’ and τ’ are the metre's. πρὸς δύσιν sets the sun low, which is what makes the shadow long — the whole plot is in that clause. A πλέθρον is a hundred Greek feet, some thirty metres. ἁπλῶς belongs with πάντων, 'all without exception', not with the verb. δέδοικα is a perfect with present force, 'I am in fear'. ⟨ποτ’⟩ is Chambry's own supplement, his mark for a word he adds.

sentences.t:
Λύκον δὲ γαυρωθέντα καρτερὸς λέων
ἑλὼν κατήσθι’· ὁ δ’ ἐβόησε μετανοῶν·
« Οἴησις ἡμῖν πημάτων παραιτία. »
sentences.tr:
Lykon de gaurōthenta karteros leōn
helōn katēsthi’· ho d’ eboēse metanoōn·
« Oiēsis hēmin pēmatōn paraitia. »
sentences.l: But a mighty lion, having seized the wolf now made-proud, was devouring him; and he, repenting, cried out: « Self-conceit is for us a part-cause of our sufferings. »
sentences.i: But a strong lion caught the wolf in his new-found pride and set about eating him; and the wolf cried out, when it was too late to think again: « It is our own conceit that helps to bring our sufferings on us. »
sentences.n: γαυρωθέντα is the aorist passive of γαυρόω, the same verb Chambry uses in the title he supplies. κατήσθι’ is κατήσθιε, imperfect, elided before the following vowel: the lion is in the middle of eating him while he speaks. μετανοέω is to think again afterwards, to change one's mind. παραίτιος, feminine to agree with οἴησις, is the part-cause, the thing that has a hand in the result; ἐστί is left unexpressed, as regularly. Chambry prints no separate moral for this fable — the wolf's closing line serves as one.
